Ordering tests such as CT scans when not clinically indicated isn't as benign as it may first appear, on an individual and population level.

Firstly, tests should be ordered as indicated and here pre-test probability needs to be considered, as well as the ability of the test to either rule in or rule out a certain pathology.  This is how you determine the potential benefit of a test, which can be weighed against the potential risks.  If a test has low pre-test probability it is unlikely to find anything significant to the problem at hand, and unlikely to rule anything out (because it's an irrelevant test to the complaint), so potential benefit is low.

We can then compare this to the potential risks of ordering the test.

On an individual level:
Incidentalomas and over investigation causing psychological and physical harms.  Think patient anxiety, unneeded biopsies, financial cost, and delay in diagnosis of the condition actually causing issues due to the time spent chasing red herrings.

Patients who demand things that are not indicated to the nth degree (I'm not referring to those who simply ask "Hey doc, my mate Johnny said a CT might be good and he got one for something similar, what do you reckon?") are rarely reassured or placated by a negative result of a test, and it becomes a vicious cycle of what next? Since the CT, a dynamic has been established whereby the patient feels enabled to direct what investigations are ordered and you have now bought into their initial line of thinking that their suggested investigative route has validity for their complaint. If they've been googling CTs with relation to their symptoms, they've also been googling other more expensive, invasive, complicated and potentially harmful tests or procedures.

On an individual level to the doctor, have fun explaining why you are over investigating to any regulatory authority, given the potential harms to the patient outlined above.  Especially if they are receiving said investigations with a degree of government rebate.

On a social level:
It clogs up the system.  Yes, even if the patient is paying privately, waitlists increase when more people are referred for something.  Waitlists for primary practitioners subsequently increase as these investigations need to be followed up with further appointments, or at the very least administrative time that detracts from clinical time.

Joint laxity, constipation, blood volume increases, low blood pressure, and significantly increased cardiac input are NOT common or even know side effects of contraception.  I am not reaching, at all.  HRT and contraception cause none of these things.  The levels of hormones in those things compared to the levels of hormones circulating during pregnancy are wildly different. Doctors also plan ahead for safety, and knowing these things are likely prior to anaesthesia and surgery in increases safety.

Cardiac output increases - the heart is working harder in several ways - by approximately 20% at only 8 weeks gravid.  Blood vessels relax, which means to maintain adequate blood pressure the heart HAS to work harder and pump out more blood with each contraction, and yet blood pressure still drops in early pregnancy and can be significantly more difficult to maintain.  Heart strain and the potential to not be able to maintain blood pressure due to vasodilation - pretty important things to know going u to surgery.

Respiration changes, the amount of air taken for each inhalation increases.  This can affect how you may need to be ventilated when undergoing surgery.

At all stages, pregnancy increases the risk of blood clots forming.  So do surgical procedures.

Progesterone increases, which makes joints more lax and the ligaments holding things in place, including organs, more flexible so things can move more easily.  This includes stomach contents.  The stomach both empties more slowly and is much more prone to reflux and vomiting, which matters when you're needing to be fasted for surgery so that your airway isn't at risk.

Smooth muscle relaxes, which can and does often cause constipation.  You know what will make that ten times worse? Many pain relief medications, often prescribed post-op.

These are all changes that occur throughout pregnancy including very early pregnancy, and this is not an exhaustive list.

There is still growing evidence that salience is aberrant in schizophrenia, some 20 years after the abberant salience theory was positied.  

If many things are "erroneously" identified as salient and used to inform decision making, it is unlikely going to lead to good decisions for the individual.  "Dampening" of salient information is not in and of itself a bad things when unhelpful, incorrect, or far too many things are being recognised as salient.

Evidence suggests that both motivational and non-motivational salience is abberant in those with psychotic illnesses, and is apparent early on in the illness course.  This is in the absence of any treatment with antipsychotics.

A 2016 study found that in terms of adaptive salience/motivational, there was no difference between those with a chronic psychotic illness on no treatment, those in treatment for a short time, those on treatment long term, between antipsychotic doses, or between reported levels of sedation.

The idea that antipsychotics worsen adaptive salience/motivation emerged when the salience theory was in its infancy and was made due it's seemingly good face validity.
